doc.title: Sol Yaged interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000

title: Recording with Chubby Jackson and Coleman Hawkins; Hawkins with Henderson
summary: Sol recalls Chubby Jackson, his Metropole-era album with Coleman Hawkins, and Hawkins in Henderson's band.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You made a record with Chubby Jackson years ago?
Oh boy, you have a good memory, yeah.
You two must have been something together.

A very funny guy. Very, very humorous. He has a good attitude and he loves to play and a great player. I don’t use that word loosely. To me that word “great” Monk is a superlative. Benny Goodman, great. Louis Armstrong, great. Teddy Wilson, great. Art Tatum, great. Jess Stacy, piano, great. Mel Powell, great. And there were some good players. But the ones I just mentioned, great. Lionel Hampton, great. Harry James, great. Ziggy Elman, great. Toots Mondello, great. Hymie Schertzer, great. Johnny Hodges, great, Coleman Hawkins, the greatest. He recorded with me, I don’t know if you know that. I made an album when I was at The Metropole, and Coleman Hawkins was an extra added attraction on my album. He helped sell my album, Monk. His name, believe me. I was very, very indebted to him, willing to record with me.
Was it a ten inch record at that time?
No I think it was a twelve inch record.
Boy I’d like to see something like that.

Yeah I think it was originally made on London Records and then it was sold to Phillips Records. I don’t even think I have a copy of it, I’ll be honest with you. Coleman Hawkins. He was unbelievable. One of a kind. When he played with Fletcher Henderson’s band in the late 20s and 30s, he stood out, as they say, like a sore thumb. That’s how powerful he was. He was just — you can’t even describe him — how he

overshadowed all the other musicians in that band, and he had some great players. Fletcher Henderson had people like Buster Bailey on clarinet and J.C. Higginbotham and Hilton Jefferson, Coleman Hawkins was something else.
